notes: Actual results for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2024, as the city reported them to the Census Bureau's Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances. Not a budget.
Some Alaska cities run their own school districts; where this one does, school spending is included and left out of the services and overhead shares.
Covers every fund, including water, sewer, electric and other utilities. Debt service counts interest and principal repaid; borrowing and transfers between funds are left out.
The city borrowed $39,852,000 during the year, which is not counted as revenue but helps explain spending above revenue.
Courts, legal services, public buildings, housing and community development count as overhead.
Debt is long-term debt outstanding plus short-term debt at year end.

Political money counts contributions from businesses, unions and registered groups (PACs) to mayor and assembly candidates, reported to the Alaska Public Offices Commission since 2023. Alaska bars businesses and unions from giving to candidates directly, so most of this money comes through their groups. Individuals, candidates' own money, in-kind gifts, and party and candidate committees are not counted.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.
Cameras: no license-plate cameras are mapped inside Municipality of Anchorage's borders in OpenStreetMap as of 2026-10-20.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-20. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals and corporate tax breaks have not been checked for Alaska yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.
